t.3.38.1: But Rāvaṇa, though addressed by Mārīca with those fitting and proper words, did not accept them, just as one who longs to die refuses medicine.
t.3.38.2: To Mārīca, who had spoken words wholesome and beneficial, the lord of the rākṣasas, driven by Time, spoke harsh and improper words.
t.3.38.3: O Mārīca, these words of improper meaning that you speak to me are utterly fruitless, like seed sown in barren saline soil.
t.3.38.4: But I cannot be shaken by your words from a battle with Rāma, a man of wicked conduct, a fool, and above all a mere mortal.
t.3.38.5: He who, having abandoned his friends, his kingdom, his mother and likewise his father, went off to the forest in a single stride upon hearing the vulgar words of a woman.
t.3.38.6: But I must surely carry off, with you at my side, Sītā, who is dearer than life to that man who slew Khara in battle.
t.3.38.7: Thus, O Mārīca, is my resolve firmly fixed in my heart; it cannot be turned back even by the gods and asuras together with Indra.
t.3.38.9: A wise minister who desires his own prosperity should speak to the king only when asked, with hands joined in reverence.
t.3.38.8: Only when asked should you speak in this way of the fault or the merit, of the danger or the means, in deciding upon this undertaking.
t.3.38.10: A lord of the earth should be addressed with words that are not contrary to his wishes, gentle from the start, auspicious and beneficial, and joined with due courtesy.
t.3.38.11: O Mārīca, a king who is worthy of honor does not welcome advice that is spoken with contempt and devoid of respect, even if it is beneficial.
t.3.38.12: Kings of boundless might bear five forms, those of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama and Varuṇa: the heat of Agni, the valor of Indra, the gentleness of Soma, the punishing rod of Yama, and the graciousness of Varuṇa.
t.3.38.13: Therefore kings are to be honored and worshipped in all circumstances. But you, not understanding dharma, have given yourself over entirely to delusion.
t.3.38.14: Out of wickedness you speak such harsh words to me, who have come to you. O Rākṣasa, I do not ask you about merits and faults, nor about what is fitting for myself; rather, in this undertaking you ought to lend me your assistance.
t.3.38.15: Becoming a golden deer, dappled with spots of silver, and luring Vaidehī, you may then go wherever you please.
t.3.38.16: But seeing you as a golden illusory deer, Maithilī, filled with wonder, will quickly say to Rāma, "Bring this one to me!"
t.3.38.17: And when Kākutstha and Lakṣmaṇa have gone away, I shall carry off Vaidehī at my ease, as the thousand-eyed one carried off Śacī.
t.3.38.18: Having thus accomplished this task, go wherever you wish, O Rākṣasa. I shall give you half of the kingdom, O Mārīca of good vows.
t.3.38.19: Go, gentle one, along an auspicious path for the furtherance of this undertaking. Having deceived Rāghava and obtained Sītā without a battle, I shall return to Laṅkā together with you, my purpose accomplished.
t.3.38.20: This task of mine you shall certainly carry out, even if by force; for one who stands opposed to the king never prospers in happiness.
t.3.38.21: Once you encounter him, your life will be in peril, and death is surely certain for me this very day if I oppose him. Weigh this carefully with your intellect, and then do whatever is wholesome in this matter.
